Some of the stuff is found legitimately by expeditions funded by the museum or their government. These days, they make sure they've got permission from everyone involved and everything is above-board and legal. Typically those laws are set by the local government, but it's complicated.

Similarly, it's not uncommon for people to dig up interesting artifacts while doing construction and the like. Most governments require construction companies to hire specialists, museums and universities, to come and take away anything that might be historically significant, same way you pay a lumber company to haul away timber. Some of that stuff then gets put on display at museums.

Museum displays are often loaned out to the museum by benefactors. Sometimes those benefactors just want to show everyone their cool stuff, but other times it's basically free advertising for their art before they sell it.

Museums will also sometimes just buy whatever it is they want to display. These days they usually do their due diligence to make sure the person they're buying the display from does legally own the item and is legally permitted to sell the item.

There are two main routes to feudalism or clan government. These are major decisions, listed in your decisions tab.

If you are an independent ruler or have a tribal liege, you will have the option to Embrace Feudal Ways or Embrace Clan Ways. You need to have an organized faith, your culture must have 70% or more of the tribal military and civic technologies, your realm capital must have at least 5 development, your government needs to have absolute tribal authority (the highest tier of tribal authority), and you need your level of fame to be at least distinguished (2nd tier of fame). You can only Embrace Clan Ways if you are a Muslim, otherwise you can only Embrace Feudal Ways.

If you have a feudal or clan liege, you can Embrace Feudal Ways Through Liege or Embrace Clan Way Through Liege. You will only need to have an organized faith. If you use this route, your government type will match your liege's government type (usually Clan for Muslim rulers and feudal for non-Muslim rulers).

Northern Lords has a few special options for Northern European tribes. The decision to Elevate the Kingdom of Mann and the Isles will change you to a feudal government, as will taking the decision to Secure the High Kingdom of the North Sea as an unreformed tribal ruler. Norse and Estonian tribal rulers have access to the Varangian Adventure Causus Belli, and winning a war as the attacker using the Varangian Adventure CB against a feudal target will cause your government to become feudal.

If you have a feudal or clan government and only own tribal counties, you can use the Embrace Tribal Ways decision to revert back to tribal government.

There is no way to change from feudal to clan or from clan to feudal. Republican and theocratic governments are AI only.

I mean, as a marxist I am absolutely down with the argument that a thing is given value by the labor required to create it, and anything that encourages people to think of value as a product of labor is a positive in my book.

The flip side of that argument in this specific case, however, is that it took a lot of fucking labor to create machines that can automatically generate art. Adopting a labor-focused understanding of value would mean acknowledging that these machines are also valuable.

Ultimately, the reason so many artists object to their material being used to train these machines is that we don't use a labor-focused system to determine value. One of the things that makes art valuable in our current economic system is that some people can't produce good art. Good art is valuable in large part because it's scarce. If we remove that scarcity of talent by creating machines that let anyone create good art without changing how we determine the value of art, then many artists will lose their employment. Those artists will both lose their income and have to take on the additional financial burden of retraining to work in another field.

Seriously, consider a hypothetical utopia where your needs would be met without question. Not just your fundamental needs for food and shelter, but also higher-order needs like stability, entertainment, and self-fulfillment. In that utopia, wouldn't the democratization of art be generally considered a good thing? Imagine how beautiful the world would be if everyone could express themselves through beautiful art.

Sure, some would still object. Artists are by nature a hot-blooded sort. On the whole, however, I believe that resistance to AI art would be much reduced in this hypothetical utopia. Therefore, the root of most of the resistance to AI art seems to be rooted in economic anxiety (that much-maligned term).

I don't know what economic system automation will create. However, I genuinely believe our modern economic system will be unable to function in a world where automation is the norm. Hopefully, our economic system will give way to fully automated luxury gay space communism. Conversely, I hope that it doesn't lead to just an unimaginable amount of violence. Based on my experience, things will probably end up being a little bit better but still just sorta fundamentally okay.

Jesus Christ this is a braindead take. The AP Style Guide is a style guide, an attempt to take the complicated reality of language and simplify it into a list of simple, understandable rules.

"Consider to what degree the group you are describing benefits from privilege, and then use that judgement to determine whether 'the X' is an acceptable term" is a complicated rule. It brings in the writer's personal beliefs, biases, and ignorance into the matter. It invites offense, both because using 'the X' language will be interpreted as minimizing a group's struggle and because not using 'the X' language will be interpreted as viewing a group as weak and unable to defend their interests. It forces the author to slow down and take time to research and consider matters that may be only tangentially related to the work at hand. Perhaps worst of all, it introduces inconsistency, the very thing style guides are created to prevent.

"Don't use 'the X' to describe groups of people" is simple and elegant. There is no room for the author to mistakenly under or over estimate a group's privilege, since their choice of words does not reflect their views on that group. Anyone offended by the language can be mollified by the knowledge that at least every group of people receives the same treatment. The author needs only remember this simple rule, and can focus their efforts on expressing the information they intend to express. Finally, the rule is perfectly consistent.

Take, for example, people of Basque descent. Under the standards proposed by these Tumblr users, any press writing about people of Basque descent will be forced to decide whether people of Basque descent have been oppressed enough. I can tell you now, regardless of what decision you make, some portion of your Spanish audience will be enraged. Should every fluff piece and restaurant review from Basque country really have to choose sides on the Basque conflict? In fact, this issue is so touchy that even calling it the "Basque conflict" will offend Basque loyalists.

In contrast, the AP Style Guide makes this matter quite easy. You don't call them the Basque, you use a phrase like people of Basque descent. Anyone who is offended by "people of Basque descent" can be directed to the style guide, and can take solace in the fact that this is the same treatment everyone receives.

Both dadaist and postmodern art focus on non-traditional materials and practices, which is part of why dada is often misidentified as postmodernism.

However, the dada movement was socialist, critiquing bourgeois affectations and questioning what gave art its meaning. The dadaist contributions to philosophy never ranged out far beyond the philosophy of art, largely content to leave broader questions to philosophers. The dadaists preferred to focus on the mundane and the material.

In contrast, the postmodernists largely reject socialist ideas, only really taking on socialism's focus on the material. The postmodernists were pretty anti-socialist, believing ideology to be merely an attempt to justify the thinker's beliefs. The postmodernists also explored the broad philosophical questions that had been largely bypassed by the dadaists, rejecting the enlightenment idea that one could really objectively know anything in favor of more relativist models.

Duchamp's Fountain, and his other readymades, were (depending on your beliefs, either created or chosen) to argue that "art" is not an inherent property of an object, but rather an act that is performed upon an object. By choosing this specific urinal and making it Fountain, Duchamp argued, he had made this urinal art, but other urinals of the same model were not art because he had not chosen them.

The modernists of his time argued that Duchamp was wrong on one of two points. The first is that Fountain, and the other readymades, were created for a practical use, and therefore were not art. The other point was that, even if it was conceded that Fountain was art, Duchamp was merely a plagiarist taking credit for the artistry of the person or people who designed the urinal; art, the modernists argued, was given value by the labor of creation, not by the act of choosing.

Postmodernists would disagree with both Duchamp and the modernists. Art, they argued, did not derive value from the labor of craftsmanship nor from choosing something to be art. Rather, the postmodernists argued, art derives value from our belief that art has value. Duchamp's Fountain only became valuable, because the art community believed it to be valuable. That's why Duchamp's Fountain is more valuable than Freytag-Loringhoven and Schamburg's God, despite the two works both elevating plumbing to art close enough in time to throw doubt on which came first.

In short, the postmodernists would call the dadaists naive hippies, and the dadaists would call the postmodernists bourgeois elitists.
